title: Krishna and the Three Strands
hookLine: Arjuna asks Krishna how to spot someone free of the three gunas, and the answer reaches the kitchen
carry: the three gunas weave every mood and meal
tomorrow: the gods win a battle, and a blade of grass

lines: ARJUNA ASKS: HOW WOULD I KNOW THEM?
THEY DON'T HATE THE HEAVY DAY.
cards: Two armies wait. In the chariot between them, Krishna is teaching Arjuna, and in the fourteenth chapter of the Bhagavad Gita he names three forces, born of nature, that tie every embodied being to the world.
Arjuna, a practical man, asks the practical question: how would I recognize someone who has gone beyond them? How do they act? Krishna's answer surprises.

That person, he says, doesn't hate clarity, or restless activity, or even confusion when it comes, and doesn't long for any of them when it goes. They sit like someone looking on, and know: it's only the strands, moving.

teach.b: Those three are the gunas, and Samkhya puts them at the heart of prakriti. Guna is often translated strand or quality. The Samkhya Karika describes them in a single verse.
Sattva is light, and shows things: the morning every page lands. Rajas stirs and moves: the morning you check your phone, refill your water and plan the whole semester.
Tamas is heavy, and covers: the paragraph you read four times. Everything on prakriti's side, a stone, a meal, a mood, is some mix of the three. They aren't heroes and villains.

The Karika says they lean on one another and take turns on top, working together the way a lamp does; commentators spell it out as oil, wick and flame making one light. And this teaching lives in Hindu kitchens.

In the Gita's seventeenth chapter, Krishna sorts food by the gunas: wholesome, pleasing food that brings long life, strength and cheer is dear to the sattvic; food too bitter, sour, salty or burning, to the rajasic; stale, leftover food, to the tamasic.

That's why many Hindu families speak of a sattvic meal, and why many cook without onion and garlic for puja or on fast days, a later custom that counts those two as stirring or heavy. It lives in hard mornings too.
Krishna's free person doesn't hate the heavy day.
She knows it's the strands, and strands take turns.

how: Many Hindu teachers use the three gunas, sattva, rajas and tamas, to speak about food, moods and habits, following the Bhagavad Gita (chapters 14 and 17). Many families keep puja and fast-day food sattvic, and some leave out onion and garlic, a later custom built on the same idea.

o: a set of three prayers said at fixed hours
a teaching on the three ages of a person's life
a teaching that the world is woven of three strands

games.q: the three strands — tap the pairs.

s: in Samkhya, tamas is the bad guna to get rid of
the Karika says the three work together, each leaning on the others, like oil, wick and flame.
in the Gita, Krishna sorts food by the three gunas
chapter 17: wholesome food that brings strength and cheer for the sattvic, sharp and burning for the rajasic, stale for the tamasic.
the gunas belong to purusha, the witness
they're the strands of prakriti, everything that is seen.

games.q: your cousin drags through a whole family puja, and an aunt sighs, "so tamasic." by Krishna's answer to Arjuna, what fits?
o: tamas is on top for now; the strands take turns, and nobody is only one guna.
she's a tamasic person, and always will be.
games.why: Krishna's free person doesn't hate heaviness when it comes. everything on prakriti's side is a mix, and the mix shifts.

practice: Check in with what's here right now: something restless, an urge to move or plan; something heavy, a fog or a pull toward sleep; something clear. No score; just notice the mix, and that it shifts.
Then, at your next meal, pause before the first bite. Many Hindus offer the food first, some with the Gita's verse that begins brahmarpanam. If you pray, offer the plate in your own words.
If you don't, simply look at it with thanks.

wordCard.voice: Samkhya. The school that sees prakriti woven from three gunas: sattva, clear; rajas, moving; tamas, heavy. Together, like oil, wick and flame, they make one light.

orig.note: Sanskrit: one of the three gunas, the strands or qualities that prakriti is made of in Samkhya.

carryVoice: Your line: the three gunas weave every mood and meal. They take turns; let them. See you tomorrow.

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 14.5 (sattva, rajas and tamas, born of prakriti, bind the embodied)

Bhagavad Gita 17.8–10 (foods dear to the sattvic, rajasic and tamasic)
Bhagavad Gita 4.24 (brahmarpanam, often said before meals)
